name: AI for Communication and Family Connection
objectives: Using a free AI assistant, ask for a family message draft that says who it is for, what it is about, the tone and the length, so the first draft fits the person
Given an AI draft, change the draft so it sounds like you and add one personal detail, so it reads naturally when you say it out loud
Given a finished message in the AI app, copy it and paste it into a text or email, then send it, to the right person, checked before you tap Send
Given a video call or link from a family member, join the call and turn the microphone and camera on, with your face clearly seen and heard
Using your phone or tablet camera, take a photo and share it with a family member with a short caption, without help

When a message or call says a family member is in trouble and needs money, spot the warning signs of a family emergency scam and check by calling a number you already have, sending no money or codes before you check

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Using AI to help write a family message
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Ask an AI assistant to draft a short message for a family member.
This lesson builds toward: Using a free AI assistant, you will ask for a family message draft that says who it is for, what it is about, the tone and the length, so the first draft fits the person.
Sometimes the hardest part of keeping in touch is knowing what to say. An AI assistant such as ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot or Google Gemini can write a first draft for you in seconds.
Tell it who the message is for, what it is about, and how you want it to sound. For example: "Write a short, cheerful text to my grandson Leo, who just finished his first week of college. I am proud of him. Keep it under 40 words."
The draft is a starting point, not the final word. You know your family; the assistant does not.
Step by step:
- Open your AI assistant.
- Say who the message is for and what it is about.
- Say how it should sound: cheerful, gentle, funny or simple.
- Say how long it should be.
Words to know:
- Draft: a first version of a message that you can change before you send it.
- Tone: how a message sounds, such as warm, funny or serious.
Try it now: Think of one family member you would like to hear from. Ask an assistant to write a short, warm message to them about something real, such as a birthday, a new job or a simple hello.
You can now ask an AI assistant to draft a short message for someone you love.

check.q: What is an AI draft of a message?
options: The final message the AI sends for you
A starting point you can change
check.why: The draft is a starting point; you know your family and the assistant does not.

check.q: You want a message for your granddaughter's birthday. What do you tell the assistant?
options: Who it is for, what it is about, how it should sound and how long it should be
Her home address and phone number
check.why: Saying who, what, the tone and the length gets a draft that fits.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Making the message sound like you
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Change an AI draft so it sounds like your own voice.
This lesson builds toward: Given an AI draft, you will change the draft so it sounds like you and add one personal detail, so it reads naturally when you say it out loud.
AI drafts can sound a little stiff or too fancy. Your family will notice if it does not sound like you, so make it yours.
You can ask the assistant: "Make it sound more casual." "Use shorter words." "Add that I am making his favorite apple pie when he visits." Or you can simply change the words yourself.
Add one detail only you would know: a nickname, a memory, an inside joke. That is what makes a message feel personal.
Step by step:
- Read the draft out loud.
- Mark any words you would never say.
- Ask for a change, or change the words yourself.
- Add one personal detail only you know.
Words to know:
- Personal detail: something specific to you and the person, like a memory or nickname.
Try it now: Take your draft from Lesson 1. Read it out loud, make one change so it sounds like you, and add one personal detail.
You can now turn an AI draft into a message that sounds like you.

check.q: Why change an AI draft before you send it?
options: The AI makes every message too short
So it sounds like you, because your family will notice if it does not
Because AI drafts are always rude
check.why: AI drafts can sound stiff; making them yours keeps them personal.

check.q: Your draft is fine but feels plain. What do you add?
options: A detail only you would know, like a nickname or a memory
check.why: A nickname, memory or inside joke makes a message feel personal.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Sending your message by text or email
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Copy your message and send it by text message or email.
This lesson builds toward: Given a finished message in the AI app, you will copy it and paste it into a text or email, then send it, to the right person, checked before you tap Send.
Once your message is ready, you need to move it from the AI assistant to your text or email app. You do this by copying and pasting.
To copy on a phone or tablet: press and hold your finger on the text until a menu appears, then tap Copy. Many AI apps also show a small copy button under the answer. On a computer, select the text with the mouse, then right-click and choose Copy.
Then open your Messages or email app, start a new message to your family member, press and hold in the message box and tap Paste (on a computer, right-click and choose Paste). Read it one last time and send it.
Step by step:
- Copy the message: press and hold, then tap Copy, or use the copy button.
- Open your Messages or email app.
- Start a new message to your family member.
- Press and hold in the message box and tap Paste.
- Read it once more, then tap Send.
Words to know:
- Copy and paste: picking up text from one place and putting it in another, without retyping.
- Text message: a short written message sent from one phone to another.
Try it now: Copy your finished message from Lesson 2 and send it to your family member by text or email.
You can now copy a message from an AI assistant and send it by text or email.

options: Puts the text you copied into a new place
check.why: You copy text in one app and paste it into the message box of another.

check.q: You have copied your message from the AI app. What do you do next?
options: Open Messages or email, start a message to them and paste it in
check.why: Open the Messages or email app, start a new message and paste the text in.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Seeing and sharing with family

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Joining a video call
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Join a video call with a family member and use the camera and microphone.
This lesson builds toward: Given a video call or link from a family member, you will join the call and turn the microphone and camera on, with your face clearly seen and heard.
A video call lets you see and hear someone at the same time, from anywhere. Common free apps include FaceTime (on iPhone and iPad), WhatsApp, Google Meet and Zoom. Families often pick the one most of them already use.
The easiest way to start is to let a family member call you. When the call comes, tap the green button or Accept. If they send you a link, tap the link at the agreed time and then tap Join.
Once you are in the call, find the microphone and camera buttons. If a button has a line through it, it is off; tap it to turn it on. Hold the device at eye level with light in front of you, not behind you, so they can see your face.
Step by step:
- Agree on a time and app with your family member.
- When the call comes, tap Accept, or tap the link they sent and tap Join.
- Check that the microphone and camera are on.
- Hold the device at eye level with light in front of you.
- Tap the red button to end the call.
Words to know:
- Video call: a call where you can see and hear each other on screen.
- Link: blue or underlined text you tap to go somewhere, such as a call.
- Mute: turning off your microphone so others cannot hear you.
Try it now: Ask a family member to call you on the app they use. Answer it, check your camera and microphone are on, say hello, then end the call with the red button.
You can now join a video call, turn your camera and microphone on and off, and end the call.

options: A call where you see and hear each other at the same time
check.why: A video call lets you see and hear someone at the same time, from anywhere.

check.q: On a video call, your family says they cannot see your face clearly. What do you change?
options: Sit with a bright window behind you
Hold the device at eye level with light in front of you
check.why: Eye level and light in front of you let them see your face.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Sharing a photo with family
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Take a photo and send it to a family member.
This lesson builds toward: Using your phone or tablet camera, you will take a photo and share it with a family member with a short caption, without help.
Sharing photos is one of the best ways to stay close. You can send a picture of your garden, a meal you cooked or a page from an old photo album.
Open the Camera app, point at what you want, and tap the large round button. To send it, open the Photos or Gallery app, tap the photo, then tap the Share button (often a square with an arrow, or three dots joined by lines). Choose Messages, email or WhatsApp, then choose your family member.
An AI assistant can help you write a caption, such as: "Write a short, fun caption for a photo of my first ripe tomato of the summer."
Step by step:
- Open the Camera app and tap the round button.
- Open Photos or Gallery and tap the photo.
- Tap the Share button.
- Choose Messages, email or WhatsApp, then your family member.
- Add a few words and send.
Words to know:
- Share button: a button that sends a photo or page to someone else.
- Caption: a short line of words that goes with a photo.
Try it now: Take a photo of something you are proud of. Ask an AI assistant for a short caption, then send the photo with the caption to a family member.
You can now take a photo, add a caption, and share it with family.

check.q: What does the Share button do in the Photos app?
options: Lets you send the photo by Messages, email or WhatsApp
check.why: Tap the photo, tap Share, then choose how and to whom to send it.

check.q: You want a few fun words to go with a photo of your garden. What can you do?
options: Ask an AI assistant to write a short caption
Send the photo with no words ever
check.why: An AI assistant can help you write a short caption for a photo.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Staying safe in family messages
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Spot a fake "family emergency" message and check it safely.
This lesson builds toward: When a message or call says a family member is in trouble and needs money, you will spot the warning signs of a family emergency scam and check by calling a number you already have, sending no money or codes before you check.
Scammers sometimes pretend to be a grandchild or relative in trouble. They may text from a new number ("Hi Grandma, I lost my phone") or even use AI to copy a voice on the phone. They usually ask for money fast, often by gift card, wire transfer or payment app, and ask you to keep it secret.
Real family can wait a few minutes while you check. Hang up or stop replying, then call your family member, or their parent, on the number you already have saved.
Some families agree on a secret family word that only they know, to use in an emergency. Never send money until you have spoken to the person on a number you trust. You can report scams to the Federal Trade Commission at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
Step by step:
- Notice the signs: new number, rush, money request, keep it secret.
- Stop replying or hang up.
- Call your family member on the number you already have.
- Agree on a family code word for emergencies.
- Report scams at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
Words to know:
- Grandparent scam: a trick where someone pretends to be a grandchild in trouble to get money.
- Code word: a secret word your family agrees on to prove who is really calling.
Official sources:
- FTC: How to avoid a scam
- FTC: Report fraud
Try it now: Final task: ask an AI assistant to help write a short, warm message inviting a family member to a video call. Make it sound like you, send it by text or email, and join the call at the agreed time. While you talk, agree on a family code word.
You can now stay in touch with family by message, photo and video call, and check a suspicious "family" message safely.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Clear request to the AI The prompt only says "write a message". The prompt says who it is for, that it is a video call invitation, the tone and the length. The first draft needed almost no changes. Sounds like you Sent the AI draft exactly as it was. Made at least one change so it sounds like you. Added a personal detail only you would know, such as a nickname or memory. Sent to the right person The message was not sent, or went to the wrong person. Copied, pasted and sent the message by text or email to the right person. Checked the name and the words once more before sending. Joined the call Could not join, or the microphone or camera stayed off. Joined at the agreed time with microphone and camera on, and said hello. Held the device at eye level with good light and ended the call with the red button. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What is a family code word?
options: A word only your family knows, to prove who is calling in an emergency
The name of your video app
check.why: Some families agree on a secret word to check who is really calling.

check.q: A voice that sounds like your grandson asks you to send money fast and keep it secret. What do you do first?
options: Send the money and ask later
Stop and call your grandson or his parent on the number you already have
Give them the code from your phone
check.why: Rushing, secrecy and money requests are scam signs; call back on a number you trust.
